title: The Marshmallow Test Was Never About Willpower

beats.text: Scientists once thought one marshmallow could predict a child's future.
Here's the test. A kid sits alone with one marshmallow.
Eat it now, or wait fifteen minutes and get two.
Imagine you're four. The clock ticks. That marshmallow is staring at you.
Some kids cover their eyes. Some sing. Some just stare.
Years later, the kids who waited seemed to do better at school.
So it was all willpower, right? Then, in two thousand twelve, researchers changed one thing.
Before the test, an adult promised the kids fancy art supplies.
For half the kids, she came back with them.
For the other half, she came back empty-handed and said sorry.
Kids who'd been let down waited about three minutes.
Kids who'd seen a kept promise waited about twelve.
Same test. Same marshmallow. Four times the patience.
You see, waiting isn't just willpower.
It's whether you believe the second marshmallow is really coming.
And nobody waits for a promise they don't believe.

facts.claim: The marshmallow task (Mischel, Stanford): one treat now or two if the child waits, up to fifteen minutes; later follow-ups linked longer waiting to better school results such as SAT scores

University of Rochester study (Kidd, Palmeri, Aslin, Cognition, published 2012): 28 children aged three to five; before the task an experimenter promised better art supplies and either returned with them (reliable) or returned empty-handed and apologised (unreliable)
Unreliable group waited about three minutes on average, reliable group about twelve minutes, roughly four times longer

caption:
The marshmallow test was famous for measuring willpower. Then one small change made kids wait four times longer: a kept promise.
Patience follows trust.
